If You Have Been Diagnosed with a Vascular Tumor or Vascular Malformation (Vascular Anomaly)…

You or a family member have been diagnosed with a “vascular tumor / vascular malformation(recently also calledvascular (myaku)malformation”), and you are likely feeling various worries about treatment, the future, and more. We arethe diagnosis of vascular tumors and malformationsandnew drug therapiesa group of doctors and researchers studyingresearchgroup(called a “research group”).

Vascular tumors and malformations include many different conditions. Even under the same diagnosis, the course and treatment vary from patient to patient, making it difficult to find the information each individual needs.
Here, forpatientsandhealthcare professionalsand, we explain the conditions, treatments, and more,presenting the latest information as clearly as possible.。

What is the difference between “vascular malformation (kekkan kikei)” and “vascular anomaly (myakkan kikei)”?

Both terms are correct, but“vascular anomaly (myakkan kikei)” is a broader term that includes “vascular malformation (kekkan kikei)”.

The term “vascular tumors and malformations (kekkanshu / kekkan kikei)” has long been widely used in academic societies and clinical practice, and it is still used today in the names of societies and in textbooks. Recently, however, because “vascular malformation (kekkan kikei)” does not include “lymphatic malformation,”the term “vascular anomaly (myakkan kikei),” which uses “vascular (myakkan)” to cover both blood vessels and lymphatic vessels,is being used more and more. However, since it is not yet widely known, in this site we have written it as“vascular tumors and malformations (vascular anomalies)”(with “vascular anomaly” noted supplementarily where appropriate). The fact that even the name of the condition is not yet fully settled gives a sense of how challenging this condition can be.

What kind of condition are vascular tumors and malformations (vascular anomalies)?

Most are masses of blood vessels or lymphatic vessels that are present at birth or appear during childhood. Among them, “vascular tumors” and “vascular malformations” differ greatly in their characteristics.

vascular tumortumorcellsgrow / shrink, so they tend to grow larger and then smaller over a short period (often within a few months to about a year).
In contrast,vascular malformation（vascular (myaku)malformation）, unlike tumors,hardly change in size, and they never disappear. Over the long term, they are said to enlarge as the body grows, and they can also worsen following triggers such aspubertyandpregnancy、infection、injury.

Each condition is given a different name according to its characteristics. Depending on where it occurs, its size, and its symptoms, treatment may last a long time. A condition with no good treatment that is hard to cure is called “intractable,” and the major conditions among vascular tumors and malformations are designated as “childhoodchronicspecifieddiseases”“designatedintractable diseases”, which means you may also be able to receivemedical expensesubsidies. On the other hand, some people have few symptoms and no problems, and receive no particular treatment.

　Also, because the timing, location, and symptoms of onset differ, patients are often seen in a variety ofmedical departments. These include pediatrics, pediatric surgery, plastic surgery, radiology, dermatology, orthopedics, otolaryngology, and more.Comprehensive treatment tailored to each patient, drawing on the expertise of each specialty,may also be needed.

vascular tumor(tumor)vs. vascular malformations: differences and treatments
  Vascular tumor (tumor) Vascular malformation (vascular anomaly)
Condition name Infantile hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma), congenital hemangioma, other tumors, etc. Capillary malformation (port-wine stain), venous malformation (cavernous hemangioma), lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma), arteriovenous malformation, combined vascular malformation, etc.
Time of onset Mainly in infancy
(congenital hemangiomas are already present right after birth)		 Usually present at birth or appearing in infancy.
Occasionally may appear in adulthood.
Growth (how it grows) Rapid. May then shrink. Barely grows.
May gradually enlarge as the body grows.
Location and symptoms Can occur anywhere in the body (except the brain and spinal cord). Symptoms vary depending on location and size. They can affect not only appearance but also nearby organs significantly.
Treatments If it causes no problems, doctors may simply wait for it to shrink.
Depending on the location and size, drug therapy, laser treatment, and other options may be used.		 Varies by condition and symptoms, including surgery, laser treatment, sclerotherapy, and more.
Drug therapy may also be used.

How is each condition diagnosed?

In many cases, a diagnosis can be made based on thetime of onset(at birth, in infancy, in childhood, in adulthood, etc.),thecourse after onset(whether it grows, shrinks, or stays the same),、appearance(flat or raised, red or bluish-black),、palpation findings(soft or firm),、and shape, among other factors.
Sometimes, when the blood or lymphatic vessels lie deep in the body and cannot be seen from the outside or are hard to assess, a diagnosis is made through more detailed testing.
Even so, some conditions are hard to diagnose right away. Even specialists with extensive experience in vascular tumors and malformations can find the diagnosis uncertain.
Nevertheless, an accurate diagnosis is extremely important because it leads to the correct treatment.
If troubling symptoms persist,consult your regular doctoranda specialist(aspecialistin the relevant department, or refer to thewebsite of the Japanese Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies, which lists anationwide directory of facilities that treat vascular tumors and malformations). Please also consider seeing such a specialist.

What treatments are available?

Treatments includesurgical treatment（excision, etc.),as well assclerotherapy、embolization、laser therapy、drug therapy、compression therapyand more. While treatments are somewhat established for each condition, there are still many conditions for which no standard treatment has been set.
For some conditions, treating at the right time can yield very good results. In some cases, several treatments are combined.
Also, not every patient needs treatment. Some conditions heal on their own, and when treatment is expected to cause problems such asside effects、lasting complications, the condition may simply bemonitored over timewithout treatment.It is best to proceed while consulting closely with your doctor.。

Are there any new medicines?

Recent research has revealed a great deal about these conditions.
In addition, rather than removing them with surgery,new medicines taken orally that suppress the underlying cause of the conditionare being developed. Some medicines have also completedclinical trialsin Japan and have beenapproved.

On this website, the “research group studying medicines for vascular tumors and malformations” introduces explanations of these conditions and new drug treatments as clearly as possible.
